citations.excerpt: We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection. Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to perform detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance. Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors. Compared to state-of-the-art detection systems, YOLO makes more localization errors but is less likely to predict false positives on background. Finally, YOLO learns very general representations of objects. It outperforms other detection methods, including DPM and R-CNN, when generalizing from natural images to other domains like artwork.

candidate.answer:
YOLO и RT-DETR представляют два разных подхода к детекции объектов в реальном времени, имея как сходства, так и различия.

**Сходства**:

Оба подхода ориентированы на достижение высокой скорости обработки, необходимой для приложений в реальном времени, таких как автономное вождение и видеонаблюдение. YOLO достигает этого за счет единой нейронной сети, которая предсказывает ограничивающие рамки и вероятности классов напрямую из полных изображений за одну итерацию, что позволяет обрабатывать изображения со скоростью 45 кадров в секунду (и до 155 кадров в секунду для упрощенной версии Fast YOLO) [1]. RT-DETR также нацелен на высокую скорость, позиционируя себя как первый детектор в реальном времени с прямым энд-ту-энд подходом, и достигает 108 кадров в секунду на GPU T4 [2]. Оба метода стремятся к оптимизации производительности за счет упрощения конвейера обработки.


**Различия**:

Ключевое различие заключается в архитектуре и постобработке. YOLO, как CNN-архитектура, традиционно полагается на алгоритм подавления немаксимумов (NMS) для удаления дублирующих рамок, что может замедлять работу и вносить нестабильность [2]. В отличие от этого, RT-DETR основан на трансформерах и является энд-ту-энд детектором, что позволяет ему полностью исключить NMS, устраняя связанные с ним проблемы [2]. Для повышения скорости RT-DETR использует эффективный гибридный энкодер, а для повышения точности — отбор запросов с минимальной неопределенностью, что является более сложной стратегией по сравнению с унифицированной регрессионной моделью YOLO [2].

cases.question: Summarize what is known in ws-pilot-od about one-stage detectors vs two-stage detectors, in 5–8 bullet points, and say what is uncertain.

baseline.answer:
- YOLO (You Only Look Once) represents a one-stage detector that frames object detection as a single regression problem, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation.
- One-stage detectors like YOLO are extremely fast, with the base model processing images at 45 frames per second and a smaller version (Fast YOLO) reaching 155 frames per second, making them suitable for real-time applications.
- Compared to other real-time detectors, Fast YOLO achieves more than double the mean Average Precision (mAP), indicating a favorable balance between speed and accuracy.
- Two-stage detectors such as DPM (Deformable Parts Models) and R-CNN variants typically use a disjoint pipeline involving feature extraction, region classification, and bounding box prediction, often in a sliding window fashion.
- YOLO outperforms DPM and R-CNN when generalizing from natural images to other domains like artwork, suggesting it learns more generalizable object representations.
- While YOLO is less likely to predict false positives on background, it tends to make more localization errors compared to state-of-the-art two-stage detectors like Fast R-CNN.
- The unified architecture of YOLO allows for end-to-end optimization directly on detection performance, unlike traditional methods that repurpose classifiers for detection.
- YOLO has been compared to Fast R-CNN in error analysis on VOC 2007, revealing complementary strengths and weaknesses between one-stage and two-stage approaches.

Uncertainties:
- The workspace contains only one paper (YOLOv1), so insights are limited to this single work and its immediate comparisons; broader trends across later models (e.g., YOLOv3–v8, SSD, RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN) are not represented.
- Temporal context is missing—no information about how one-stage vs two-stage trade-offs evolved with subsequent research.
- Quantitative results (e.g., exact mAP values, speed comparisons) beyond what is reported in the YOLO paper are not available in this workspace.
- There is no discussion of more recent architectural improvements or hybrid approaches that may bridge the gap between one-stage and two-stage detectors.

candidate.answer:
- YOLO (You Only Look Once) represents a one-stage object detection approach that frames detection as a single regression problem, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation.
- Unlike traditional two-stage detectors such as R-CNN or DPM, which use a disjoint pipeline involving region proposal and classification, YOLO unifies the entire detection process into a single neural network.
- This unified architecture allows YOLO to be extremely fast, processing images at 45 frames per second for the base model and up to 155 frames per second for the smaller Fast YOLO variant.
- YOLO outperforms other real-time detectors in mean Average Precision (mAP), with Fast YOLO achieving double the mAP of other real-time systems.
- Compared to state-of-the-art two-stage detectors like Fast R-CNN, YOLO makes fewer false positive predictions on background but tends to make more localization errors.
- YOLO learns generalizable object representations, enabling it to generalize better than DPM and R-CNN when applied to non-natural image domains such as artwork.
- The system contrasts with sliding-window or region-based methods like Deformable Parts Models (DPM), which rely on handcrafted features and separate classification and localization stages.

## 3. Comparison to Other Detection Systems

Object detection is a core problem in computer vision. Detection pipelines generally start by extracting a set of robust features from input images (Haar [25], SIFT [23], HOG [4], convolutional features [6]). Then, classifiers [36, 21, 13, 10] or localizers [1, 32] are used to identify objects in the feature space. These classifiers or localizers are run either in sliding window fashion over the whole image or on some subset of regions in the image [35, 15, 39]. We compare the YOLO detection system to several top detection frameworks, highlighting key similarities and differences.

## Abstract

We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection. Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to perform detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance.

Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors. Compared

cases.question: In ws-pilot-od, pick two works that discuss region proposal networks and compare how each uses proposals (balanced bullets, cite sources).

baseline.answer:
- **Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks**  
  This work introduces a Region Proposal Network (RPN) that shares full-image convolutional features with the detection network, enabling nearly cost-free region proposals. The RPN is a fully convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position, trained end-to-end to generate high-quality region proposals. These proposals are then used by the Fast R-CNN detector for final object detection, forming a unified system where the RPN tells the detection network where to look. The method achieves real-time performance and high accuracy by tightly integrating proposal generation and detection [1].

- **R-FCN: Object Detection via Region-based Fully Convolutional Networks**  
  This approach follows the two-stage detection strategy, relying on region proposals (e.g., from RPN) to identify candidate regions. However, unlike Faster R-CNN, R-FCN eliminates per-region subnetworks by using position-sensitive score maps and fully convolutional computation across the entire image. Region proposals are used to pool from these score maps in a position-sensitive manner, enabling efficient classification while maintaining translation variance. The method demonstrates competitive performance with faster inference speeds, showing that high accuracy can be achieved with minimal per-region computation [2].
